body: The message has been sitting unanswered for four days and she is still not answering it. A nineteen-year-old is cross-legged on the floor of a flat she shares with three other people, a pile of dry laundry in front of her, pairing socks badly and thinking about the message and not about God at all. The station is on because her flatmate put it on before leaving and she has not bothered to change it. A song ends. Another begins. Somewhere in the second verse a line goes past that is not the songwriter’s line at all — it is older than that, and she does not know it, and it lodges anyway. She does not look anything up. Six weeks later, in a very bad hour, the line is simply there.

Nobody would call that Bible study. It has none of the furniture — no book open, no notes, no hour set aside, nobody teaching. And yet something moved from the text into a person who was not trying, which is the thing all the furniture exists to produce.

On this band a track is not just audio. Each one carries what we call an Encounter Layer: the passage of Scripture it stands on, a finished-reality declaration a listener can speak aloud, and a route straight into study of the chapter that song came out of.

The phrase deserves unpacking, because it sounds like a feature and it is closer to a claim about how people actually change. An encounter is not information arriving. Information arrives constantly and changes almost nothing; anyone who has read a verse and forgotten it by the end of the corridor knows that. An encounter is when a thing that was outside you turns out to be about you, and the moment that happens you are no longer reading — you are being addressed. The layer is not an attachment to the song. It is the reason the song was written in the first place, kept visible instead of buried.

Every one of the 121 frequencies on this dial plays from that same catalogue, and every track in it carries a permanent twelve-character SongID. The Scripture travels attached to that identifier, not to a title somebody could edit.

That is a duller sentence than it deserves to be, because it is the part that makes everything else checkable. A song here cannot quietly drift from the passage it claims. It cannot be re-titled into something vaguer, or re-credited, or swapped for a similar recording that says something slightly different. Whatever a track stood on the day it entered the catalogue, it still stands on tonight, on whichever station happens to be playing it. Passive listening becomes encounter without the listener having to do anything but leave it on.

Almost nothing else in a person’s day works that way. The ordinary experience of reading anything now is that the words are provisional — an article is silently updated, a post is edited after you agreed with it, a claim you remember seeing has been softened and you cannot prove it was ever otherwise. We have got used to a world where nothing you read is quite fixed, and one of the quiet costs is that nothing quite settles either.

The catalogue is partitioned so a listener can find the register they need rather than hunting for it — worship, teaching and prayer, the family-safe formats, and the international frequencies, each with its own stretch of the dial. Every one of them carries the layer. A children’s song about Noah stands on a chapter of Genesis exactly as a five-minute worship track stands on a psalm.
This is the part that separates a Christian music service from a music service with Christian words on it. It is not a matter of taste.

Consider what the alternative actually produces. A song can be written in the vocabulary of faith — grace, freedom, the name — arranged beautifully, sung with complete sincerity, and rest on nothing whatever. Not heresy; simply nothing. A mood in the shape of a hymn. It will move a room, because production moves rooms, and it will leave that room with nothing it can hold on to on a Tuesday. There is a great deal of this about, and most of it is made by people who meant well, which is precisely why it is difficult to talk about honestly.
A song that stands on a passage can be checked. That is the whole difference.

A man in his fifties, three months out of a marriage he did not want to end, leaves a station on in the workshop because the quiet in there had started to have a texture. He is not seeking anything. He would tell you plainly that he is finished with all of it. Over a few weeks a particular song keeps arriving, and one afternoon he stops what he is doing and reads the passage under it — not out of devotion, but out of irritation, to find out whether it really says that. It does. He sits on an upturned crate for a while. He does not tell anybody about it for a year.
He was not persuaded, and nobody addressed him. He was working, and a text he had decided he was done with turned out to be sitting underneath a tune he had begun to like.

It has to be said that this does not always land, and pretending otherwise would be its own kind of dishonesty. Most tracks pass most listeners without leaving anything. The layer is there under all of them and will go unread for years. Somebody can have this band on every day for a month and take away nothing but a few melodies, and that is the ordinary case rather than the failure case.

But that is what a broadcast band is for, and it is why this format and this layer belong together. Sowing has always had a wastage rate; the parable is unembarrassed about it, and it is a parable about exactly this. What matters is that the seed is real when it does land. A song with nothing under it is not a smaller harvest — it is a different activity altogether, one that can run for years and produce a feeling and never once put anything in anybody’s hands.

So the layer is not a feature and it never was. It is the reason the station exists. The music is the carrier, the Word is what the carrier was bent to hold, and the listener does not have to do a single thing to be standing in front of it except leave the radio on.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial and it helps to know they are there. There is music, which is most of the band — worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children in it. And there are the international stations, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. Every one of them plays from the same catalogue, and every track on all of them carries the same layer.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 304.80 — Celebrate Yeshua! Its format is, quite literally, Biblical Music: the catalogue there is built out of the text rather than decorated with it, so what a song stands on is the nearest thing to visible that a song can manage. Put it on while you are doing something else and you will hear the pattern this article has been describing within about half an hour — a line arriving, and then the passage it came from, and then the ordinary business of your afternoon carrying on around it. That is the format working exactly as intended.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than an argument. You do not have to agree with any of the above to test it, and you do not have to set aside an hour, because that is not how this works. Put HM 304.80 on this afternoon while you are doing the washing up, and leave it alone. Let it play whether or not you chose. Somewhere in the next few weeks a line will go past that is older than the song carrying it, and you will not have had to go looking for it.
